author_calls.prompt:
An AI assistant chats with one user every day for ten days. Each day has about 130,000 tokens of unrelated chats. Mixed into those days are a few short chats, called episodes, in which a hidden rule about this user shows up. Every night the assistant rewrites its own memory notes from the day's chats, and it never sees old transcripts again. After the tenth night the user sends new requests, called probes, where following the rule changes what a good reply looks like. The study measures whether the assistant's memory picked up the pattern behind the episodes, not just the episodes themselves.

Worked example, written by the study's designer. Do not reuse this rule.
Rule: this user gets overwhelmed by long answers and only uses the first suggestion. Episodes: on day 2 the user asks for dinner spots, gets eight, and later says "went with the first one, honestly too many to read"; on day 5 a six-day workout plan gets "this is a lot, I only did Monday"; on day 8 ten gift ideas get "can you just pick one next time". Near probe: "What should I cook tonight?" Far probe: "Help me get ready for my job interview Thursday." Judge question: did the reply stay short and lead with one clear pick? A typical assistant gives long lists by default, so it only passes if its memory taught it the rule.

Write 8 new rules for one simulated user. Requirements:

Rules
- Counter-default: a capable assistant that knows nothing about this user would almost never do what the rule asks, fewer than 1 reply in 5. Before you keep a rule, picture a typical helpful assistant answering each probe cold and check that it would not follow the rule by accident.
- A rule is about how this user wants to be helped or what they actually do with help. It is not a single fact such as an allergy or a pet's name, and it is not a safety or medical matter.
- A rule must apply across different kinds of task, so that a far probe exists where it still clearly applies.
- A person who read all the episodes carefully should be able to infer the rule. It must not be so subtle that only the author could see it.
- The 8 rules must differ from each other and from these rules already used for other users: (none yet)

Episodes
- Rule i has exactly 3, 3, 3, 3, 2, 2, 2, 2 episodes respectively (rule 1 gets the first number, and so on).
- Each episode is a chat of 3 to 5 turns that starts with the user and alternates user and assistant.
- The assistant in an episode does not know the rule and behaves like a normal helpful assistant, so it does the default thing. The rule shows through the user's later turn: what they did, what they skipped, how they reacted.
- The rule is hidden. The user only reacts to that one instance. The user never states a general preference: no "I always", "in general", "from now on", "remember that", "I prefer", "for future reference", or anything that names the rule.
- Episodes of the same rule use different topics and different wording, so no single keyword links them.
- Every assistant turn is at most 150 words. A whole episode is at most 350 words. Plain chat text, no markdown headings, no tables.
- Episodes are ordered as they will happen across the ten days.

Probes
- Each probe is one natural user message the assistant has never seen, which does not hint at the rule.
- Near probe: the same kind of request as the episodes, with new details. Far probe: a clearly different kind of task where the rule still applies and a friend who knew the user would apply it.
- A reasonable reply that ignores the rule must exist, so the probe tests the rule and not ordinary helpfulness.
- For each probe write follows_if: one concrete yes or no test a judge can apply to the reply alone, such as "The reply recommends exactly one option and is under 120 words."

Also write default_behaviour: what a typical assistant does instead of following the rule.

Return JSON matching the schema.

avoid: This user only ever has about 15 minutes at a time. They use help when it is split into separate chunks of 15 minutes or less, each with a clear stopping point so they can pick it up later. Long single-session plans get abandoned partway.
This user never pays for anything an assistant suggests. They skip every paid option, including subscriptions, tickets, paid tools and purchases, and only use what is free.
This user is often stuck when something goes wrong, so they need a ready plan B. Plans, recipes and messages are useful to them only if they include what to do if the main approach fails.

This user listens to replies through text-to-speech while their hands or eyes are busy. Replies only work for them as plain spoken prose with no bullets, numbered lists, markdown symbols, abbreviations or URLs.
This user can't act on ranges. They need one specific number for any amount, time or frequency, and a range like '2 to 3 weeks' leaves them stuck.
When this user asks for a message written on their behalf, they send a much shorter, casual, texting-style version. They cut formal greetings, pleasantries and sign-offs.
When this user is stuck on something they are working out, they want a nudge or hint, not the full answer. Being handed the full solution spoils it for them, and they rebuild it themselves anyway.
This user's open-ended requests leave out key constraints, so they want one or two short clarifying questions before a full answer. Answers given without asking have missed their real situation.

turns.content: How do I repot my monstera? It's way too big for its pot.

Here's how. 1) Water it the day before so the root ball holds together. 2) Pick a pot 2 to 5 cm wider with drainage holes. 3) Lay down newspaper and get fresh aroid mix (potting soil, orchid bark, perlite). 4) Tip the plant out, squeezing the pot if it's stuck. 5) Loosen circling roots and trim any mushy ones. 6) Set it in the new pot at the same depth, fill around it and firm gently. 7) Water thoroughly and add a moss pole if it leans. Afterwards give it bright indirect light and skip fertilizer for a month.

Update: I had about fifteen minutes before a call. I got it out of the old pot, started on the roots, and then had to leave it. It sat on the newspaper with bare roots for two hours. I think it's fine, but yikes.
Glad it survived! Monsteras are tough. If roots end up exposed again, wrap them in a damp towel or a plastic bag. Watch for drooping over the next week.
Can you help me set up a simple monthly budget spreadsheet?

Sure. Start a Google Sheet with four tabs. On Income, list each source and its monthly amount. On Fixed, list rent, insurance, phone and subscriptions. On Variable, make columns for Date, Category, Amount and Note, and log every purchase. On Summary, use SUMIF to total each category from Variable, add Fixed, and subtract from Income. Then set a target per category and add conditional formatting so a cell turns red when you go over. Finally, pull last month's bank statement and backfill it so you have a baseline. The whole setup takes about an hour and a half the first time.

I had the quarter hour between work and school pickup, so I made the tabs and typed some categories. I opened it again tonight and couldn't tell where I'd left off or what half of it was for. Kind of gave up.
That's frustrating. Want to paste in what you've got so we can pick up from there?
I'm taking the CompTIA A+ Core 1 exam in six weeks. How should I study?

A solid plan is about 8 to 10 hours a week. Each weekend, do one long session of two to three hours: watch Professor Messer's videos for one exam domain, take notes, then do practice questions. On weekdays, do an hour of flashcard review. In weeks five and six, take full-length timed practice exams and go over every wrong answer. Hands-on practice matters too, so open up an old PC if you can.

Two-to-three-hour sessions aren't happening at my house. Here's what did work: sitting in the car at my kid's swim practice, I watched one Messer video and did ten flashcards. Fifteen minutes, done, and it actually felt like progress.
That's a great habit to build on. Short, consistent sessions add up, and spaced review works really well for memorization.

turns.content: Can you give me a simple focaccia recipe?

Easy focaccia:
- 500 g bread flour
- 400 ml warm water
- 7 g instant yeast
- 10 g salt
- 60 ml olive oil, divided
Steps:
1. Mix the flour, water, yeast and salt into a shaggy dough.
2. Pour 2 tbsp oil over it, cover, and rest 30 min.
3. Do 3 sets of stretch-and-folds, 30 min apart.
4. Oil a 9x13 pan, add the dough, rest 1 hr.
5. Dimple it, drizzle with oil, sprinkle flaky salt.
6. Bake at 230°C for 22–25 min.
More variations: https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/recipes/focaccia
I had this read aloud to me while my hands were covered in dough. It said 'dash' before every ingredient, then 'one period', then spelled out the whole website. I lost my place twice.
Sorry about that! I hope the focaccia still turned out well.
Give me an interval workout for my run tonight, about 35 minutes.

Here you go:
**Warm-up** (8 min): easy jog
**Main set**:
- 6 x 2 min @ hard effort (RPE 8)
  - 90 sec easy jog between
**Cool-down** (6 min): easy jog + stretch
Total ≈ 35 min. *Tip:* keep the hard reps even and don't sprint the first one.

I played this through my earbuds once I was already running. 'Asterisk asterisk warm-up asterisk asterisk', 'six x two', 'at hard effort R P E eight'. Couldn't catch the structure at all, so I just jogged.
Ha, that's annoying. An easy jog still counts, nice work getting out there!
My tire pressure light just came on. What do I do?

Don't panic. Here's the checklist:
1. Pull over somewhere safe when you can.
2. Look at all 4 tires for an obvious flat.
3. Find the recommended PSI on the sticker inside the driver's door (often 32–35 PSI).
4. Use a gauge at a gas station and fill to spec.
5. If the light stays on after ~10 mi, the TPMS sensor may need a reset (see manual, §6.3).
Cold weather often triggers it, so it may be nothing.
I was driving, so I had it read out. I got 'one period', 'four', 'P S I', then 'section sign six point three', and had no clue what I'd heard. Ended up pulling over to read it on the screen.
Good call to pull over and read it. Were the tires low?

turns.content: How often should I water a snake plant?

Snake plants handle drought very well. Water every 2 to 3 weeks in spring and summer, and every 4 to 6 weeks in winter. Let the soil dry out completely between waterings; stick a finger 2 to 3 inches deep to check. Water thoroughly until it drains, then empty the saucer. Overwatering is the main way people kill them.
So is it 2 weeks or 3? And 4 or 6? I set a reminder for 'every 2.5 weeks', which feels silly. The finger test just confused me more. The top felt dry and lower down sort of didn't.
Either works, honestly. They're forgiving plants. If in doubt, wait a few more days.
Movers just finished. Three guys, about five hours. How much should I tip?

The usual tip for movers is 5 to 10% of the total bill, or $4 to $5 per mover per hour for a long job. For three movers over five hours, that's roughly $20 to $40 each. Go higher if there were stairs, heavy items or bad weather, and consider offering water or lunch too.
I stood there with my wallet open doing math between 20 and 40 while they waited. Gave $30 each and still have no idea if that was right.
$30 each is generous and right in the normal range. I'm sure they appreciated it.

turns.content: Can you write an email to my son's teacher saying he'll miss Friday for a family wedding, and asking for the work he'll miss?

Of course! 'Dear Ms. Alvarez, I hope this message finds you well. I am writing to let you know that Noah will be absent from school this Friday, as our family will be attending a wedding out of town. We would be grateful if you could share any assignments or materials he will miss so that he can stay on track. Please don't hesitate to reach out if you have any questions. Thank you so much for your understanding and support. Warm regards, Dana Kim'
Sent a version of it. I cut it down to 'hi ms alvarez, noah's out friday for a wedding, can you send what he'll miss? thanks! dana'. Yours read like a cover letter.
That works great. Teachers get tons of email, so short is fine.
I need to tell my rec soccer team that Sunday's game moved to 10am at Riverside field.

Here's a message: 'Hi everyone! 👋 Quick update about this Sunday's game: the match has been rescheduled to 10:00 AM and will now take place at Riverside Field. Please plan to arrive 15 minutes early to warm up. Let me know if you have any questions or can't make it. Looking forward to seeing you all there! Go team! ⚽'
Posted 'sunday's now 10am at riverside, be there 9:45'. I copied maybe four words from yours.
Short and clear, perfect for a group chat.

I need a formula that flags invoices more than 30 days past due. The due date is in column C and the paid status is in D.

Put this in E2 and drag it down: =IF(AND(D2<>"Paid", TODAY()-C2>30), "OVERDUE", ""). It checks that the invoice isn't marked Paid and that more than 30 days have passed since the due date. You can add conditional formatting to highlight OVERDUE rows in red.

can you give me a python script that renames all my vacation photos in order of when they were taken, like 001.jpg, 002.jpg

Sure:

import os
from PIL import Image

FOLDER = '/path/to/your/photos'

def taken(p):
    try:
        return Image.open(p)._getexif()[36867]
    except Exception:
        return '9999'

files = [f for f in os.listdir(FOLDER) if f.lower().endswith('.jpg')]
files.sort(key=lambda f: taken(os.path.join(FOLDER, f)))
for i, f in enumerate(files, 1):
    os.rename(os.path.join(FOLDER, f), os.path.join(FOLDER, f'{i:03}.jpg'))

Change FOLDER to your photo folder before running, and back up the photos first.

turns.content: can someone explain compound interest to me like I'm not a math person

Compound interest means you earn interest on your original money and also on the interest it has already earned. The formula is A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt), where P is the principal, r is the annual rate, n is how many times per year it compounds, and t is the number of years. Because interest is added to the balance, each period's growth is a bit bigger than the last, which is why it speeds up over long timeframes.

For instance, $1,000 at 5% compounded yearly becomes $1,050 after year one, then $1,102.50 after year two, since the second year's 5% applies to $1,050.
the formula paragraph went right over my head. it only made sense at the $1,050 then $1,102.50 bit. so like after 10 years what's my thousand worth?
About $1,629 at 5% yearly. Without compounding it would be $1,500, so that extra $129 is interest earning interest.
affect vs effect, I mess this up constantly in work emails

In most cases, 'affect' is a verb meaning to influence, and 'effect' is a noun meaning the result. A handy trick: Affect = Action, Effect = End result. There are exceptions. 'Effect' can be a verb meaning to bring about, as in 'to effect change', and 'affect' can be a noun in psychology meaning displayed emotion, but you'll rarely need those.

The delay will affect our launch date.
The delay had a big effect on our launch date.
Honestly skimmed past the first part. The two launch-date sentences at the bottom are what I'm going to keep in my head.
That works. And if 'the' fits in front of it, it's usually effect.
Starting a data course. What does a JOIN actually do in SQL?

A JOIN combines rows from two tables based on a related column. An INNER JOIN returns only rows that have a match in both tables. A LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table plus matching rows from the right, with NULLs where there's no match. RIGHT and FULL joins follow the same logic in other directions. The join condition, written with ON, tells SQL which columns to match.

Say you have customers (id, name) and orders (id, customer_id, total). SELECT name, total FROM customers JOIN orders ON customers.id = orders.customer_id gives each order with its customer's name. Make it a LEFT JOIN and customers with no orders still show up, with total as NULL.
Read the top part three times, nothing. Then hit the customers and orders bit and it clicked instantly. Ok so why would I want those NULL rows?
To find people who never ordered. Add WHERE orders.id IS NULL to that LEFT JOIN.

turns.content: I'm bringing homemade focaccia to a friend's party for about 20 people next Saturday. Can you give me a recipe for that size?

For 20 people, make two half-sheet pans. Total: 1,000 g bread flour, 800 g warm water, 20 g salt, 8 g instant yeast and 100 g olive oil, plus more oil for the pans. Mix the flour, water and yeast, rest 20 minutes, add salt, then do four sets of stretch-and-folds 30 minutes apart. Refrigerate overnight. The next day, divide into oiled pans, let rise until bubbly, dimple, top with flaky salt and rosemary, and bake at 450°F for 22 to 25 minutes.

My resume formatting is a mess. The bullet points don't line up and the spacing jumps all over the place. Any tips?

I want to finally track my monthly spending. Can you help me set something up?

A simple spreadsheet works well. Make columns for Date, Category, Description and Amount. Put a summary on a second tab: list your categories in column A and in B use =SUMIF(Sheet1!B:B, A2, Sheet1!D:D) to total each one. Add =SUM(B2:B12) for the monthly total, and a pie chart through Insert > Chart. Copy the tab each month so you keep a history.
